title: FOSDEM 2027: CFP for Open Source & EU Policy Devroom
content:
The Open Source Initiative, in collaboration with APELL, Eclipse Foundation, Github, Linux Foundation Europe, Mozilla, NLNET Labs, Open Forum Europe, and OpenSSF, are delighted to invite you to submit a proposal for a talk, and join us for the 4th edition of the Open Source & EU Policy devroom at FOSDEM on Sunday, January 31st 2027, to explore how FLOSS interacts with the EU, including how ongoing and upcoming EU laws could impact the FLOSS ecosystem, what we have to gain, what we have to lose, and what needs to change.

The devroom will focus on bringing together FLOSS communities and EU lawmakers, including Members of the European Parliament, and Staff from the Parliament and the Commission, helping lawmakers improve their laws and address major challenges, such as digital sovereignty and secure, interoperable technology; while giving FLOSS communities and the Digital Commons a place to raise concerns, propose improvements and changes, and figure out how best to prepare for and respond to policy proposals.

We invite you to submit your proposals for talks by 1st December 2026 at noon CET at the latest. More details available at:

title: Opening New Paths for Open Source
content:
Dear OSI community,

The past few weeks took me from New York to Halifax to Prague, and I came home with a full notebook and a long list of follow-ups.

At UN Digital Cooperation Day (part of the 81st UN General Assembly), I joined a panel on Open Source AI to reinforce the importance of shared language and common definitions when crafting policy. Later that day I joined Creative Commons and the NYU Engelberg Center for a conversation about openness and digital sovereignty. My key message there was simple: open by itself does very little, but enables a lot. You can read more about these talks, plus the inaugural 50-in-5 Awards, in Nick Vidal’s blog post Open Enables a Lot: The OSI at UNGA81.

My next stop was Stakeholder Day as part of Open Source Congress in Halifax. It was great to connect with leaders from more than 40 foundations as they formed working groups on global collaboration, sustainability, security, regulatory policy, AI, and governance. These are big problems, and it was encouraging to see so many organizations sign up to work on them together.

title: New website reflects OSI’s evolving mission
content:
Over the years, OSI’s work has expanded beyond the Open Source Definition and licensing to encompass policy and standards, research and education, and Open Source AI. The new website brings these areas into clearer focus, making it easier for the community and our partners to discover what we do and find ways to get involved.

The new website architecture organizes OSI’s work around its major strategic areas: Licensing, Open Source AI, Policy & Standards, Research & Education, and Community.

One of the most significant changes is elevating Policy & Standards to a primary navigation category. This will make our policy positions, regulatory engagement, and work across regions and topics easier to find.

We’re also expanding the visibility of Research & Education initiatives, including our work with the Open Technology Research (OTR) Network and the development of the Open Source Licensing Education hub.

Finally, under Community, we are creating dedicated pathways for different audiences, including maintainers and developers, lawyers and legal professionals, founders and executives, nonprofits and academia, and policymakers and government.

title: Announcing the 2027 State of Open Source Survey
content:
The Open Source Initiative (OSI) has teamed up again with Perforce Zend and OpenLogic, as well as the Eclipse Foundation, for the 2027 State of Open Source Survey.

This annual survey, now in its sixth year, brings together perspectives from OSS developers, administrators, and IT leaders around the world. It examines what technologies organizations are deploying, where teams are investing, and what challenges they’re facing. In 2027, that includes taking a closer look at AI, with questions covering adoption, development priorities, and how organizations are responding to a rapidly evolving regulatory environment and increased scrutiny.

The 2026 State of Open Source Survey showed how firmly open source has become established within organizational technology stacks:

  • 98% of respondents said their organizations had either increased or maintained their use of open source software over the previous year, up from 96% in 2025.
  • Avoiding vendor lock-in was cited as the most common driver of adoption, particularly for European OSS users.

title: Open Enables a Lot: The OSI at UNGA81
content:
On Monday, September 21, with the high-level week of the 81st UN General Assembly (UNGA81) underway in New York, OSI Executive Director Duane O’Brien spoke on a UN panel about Open Source AI and joined a Creative Commons symposium on openness and digital sovereignty. The OSI also attended the inaugural 50-in-5 Awards for digital public infrastructure. Different people filled each room, but many of them were circling the same question: what does openness give people, and what does it take to make good on it?

At the Creative Commons event, Duane offered a ten-word answer: “Open by itself does very little but enables a lot.” Creative Commons later called it the line of the day. Most of what the OSI said at UNGA81 was about the distance between the two halves of that sentence.

At UN Digital Cooperation Day, organized by the UN Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies (ODET), Duane joined the panel “What is Open Source AI? Applications, Strategies and Global Cooperation.” Sarah Myers West of the AI Now Institute moderated a conversation with Duane, Kari Briski of NVIDIA, Marzieh Fadaee of Cohere Labs, Jim Zemlin of the Linux Foundation, and Rumman Chowdhury of Humane Intelligence.

title: Linux’s 35th Anniversary and the Open Frontier
content:
Dear OSI community,

I’d be remiss if I didn’t open by wishing Linux a happy 35th birthday. I can’t pretend to have accomplished nearly as much by the age of 35 as Linux has, but neither was I nurtured by such a vast community of contributors and supporters. We can’t lose sight of that. Open Source is what it is because of the people who led us here, and keep us here. We all joined the community for different reasons, but many of us stayed because of the relationships and partnerships we built along the way, connections that run deeper than the code.

I get asked almost every day about the future of Open Source. One of my consistent answers is that people who love writing code will keep wanting to write code together. I believe that’s as true today as it was before AI tools, Git, the OSI, the World Wide Web, Perl, or C entered the chat. But we’re also passing through a moment of unquestionable transition. AI tools and agents are testing our processes, policies, laws, licenses, and beliefs in real time.
creator: Nick Vidal
sourceDescription: The steward of the Open Source Definition, setting the foundation for the Open Source Software ecosystem.

title: Open Weights Are Good. Open Source Is Better.
content:
By this point, you’ve seen the news about open-weight AI models and the debate over their security, efficiency, and impact on both local and national economies. Scores of businesses have come out in support of open-weights, highlighting how they increase access to advanced AI and maintain competition in the market. This is all true, and shedding light on these arguments benefits the Open Source community. 

At the same time, we must take this moment, when openness in AI is making headlines, to educate policymakers, producers, and users of these technologies about what open-weight and Open Source AI mean for the four software freedoms: the freedom to use, study, modify, and share without the need to ask for permission from the rights holder. Those are the core tenets of the Open Source movement that power the technology we use every day. Those are the tenets that built the Open Source ecosystem with a demand-side value of $8.8 trillion. It’s those tenets that we should strive to uphold in this next phase of technological development.

title: We Must Open the Frontier: OSI, OFAI Support Calls for the U.S. to Develop More Open Models
content:
The Open Source Initiative joins the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) in supporting calls for the U.S. to develop more open models because they promote competition in AI through local control and lower costs. The OFAI is a university-led, collaborative initiative that aims to bend the arc toward human-centered, responsible, transparent, and ethical AI. Led by Carnegie Mellon University, the OFAI includes university representatives from across the country as well as nonprofit voices and individual fellows from industry and government. As the policy lead, we collaborated with other OFAI members to lay out the benefits of Open Source AI and open-weight models in comparison to closed, proprietary ones. 

The statement asserts that the U.S. needs more “focus, investment, and collaboration from the full breadth of the innovation pipeline to accelerate the development of open models. This will require a strategic approach that moves beyond the status quo, bringing together new partners, both technical and non-technical, from across industry, academia, and government.”

Link to statement:  https://www.openforumai.org/news/us-needs-more-open-models

title: OSI brings the State of the Source to All Things Open 2026
content:
The Open Source Initiative (OSI) is coming to All Things Open with a track designed to connect developers with the big policy conversations shaping our ecosystem. This year’s State of the Source looks at Open Source from several perspectives. Hear about OSI’s priorities for 2027, get a practical introduction to Open Source licensing and compliance, and discuss Open Source sustainability. We’ll also explore the latest public policy developments affecting Open Source, examine the state of Open Source AI, and discuss how OSI can strengthen Open Source education and advocacy.

All Things Open is one of the largest Open Source technology conferences in the United States, bringing together a technical and engaged audience of developers, engineers, community leaders, students, educators, executives, and other Open Source practitioners.

All Things Open 2026 takes place October 19–20 in Raleigh, North Carolina, part of the Research Triangle, one of the country’s leading centers for technology and Open Source innovation.

title: OSI Governance Survey
content:
We invite the Open Source community to participate in the OSI Governance Survey and help inform the future of OSI’s governance. The survey is an opportunity for community members and stakeholders to share their perspectives on how OSI’s Board of Directors should be selected and seated.

The Open Source Initiative (OSI) is a 501(c)(3) non-profit public benefit organization. Its Board of Directors owes primary legal and fiduciary duties to the organization and its mission to ensure strategic alignment, financial integrity, and legal compliance in stewarding the Open Source Definition (OSD) and educating/supporting/advocating for the ecosystem.

The OSI Board has created a Governance Working Group to evaluate how directors are selected and seated. Following an elections pause in early 2026, this study will inform recommendations presented to the full board in September 2026 to ensure an engaged, representative, and effective governing body that works in partnership with the staff of OSI to fulfill the mission and vision of OSI.
